reader.title: Lynching of Charles Thurber
bases: A crowd took Thurber from the Grand Forks county jail after fighting the officers and hanged him from the railroad bridge (A4, A10, A23).

A mob of 1,000 to 3,000 broke into the county jail against the sheriff's resistance and hanged Thurber without trial (A4, A23); it acted on the accusation of rape and the Globe's own correspondent wrote that 'the feelings of the community fully justify the act' (A4).

The Western Associated Press report, a Globe special telegram, the Pioneer Press dispatches and the Grand Forks Herald all independently describe the storming of the jail and the hanging from the railroad bridge (A4, A17, A20, A23).

summary.text: The lynching of Charles Thurber took place on October 24, 1882, at Grand Forks, Dakota Territory, when a crowd broke into the county jail, took Thurber, a Black barber, from the sheriff, and hanged him from the railroad bridge.
Thurber had been accused the day before of assaulting a fifteen-year-old girl and Mrs. Samuel Burbank, the wife of a railroad conductor, near Norton.
The papers dwelt on the fight with the officers and the husband's part in the hanging, and several editors defended it.

According to the first wire report, on Monday, October 23, a Black barber attacked a girl on the road and then entered the house of Conductor Samuel Burbank of the Manitoba road and assaulted Mrs. Burbank.
Threshers who pursued him shot his horse, but he escaped on foot with a knife, and the report predicted he would 'undoubtedly be lynched if caught'.
At Grand Forks citizens formed a vigilance committee and guarded the bridges to Minnesota.
That night Chief of Police Hennessy and Officer Fadden arrested him at a hotel in East Grand Forks; dispatches gave his name as Thurbane, Thurbur and Thurber.
Early on October 24 speakers urged a crowd at the city hall to wait for a hearing, but someone shouted 'Hang the nigger!' and the outer doors were battered down before the raid was called off.
In his cell Thurber told reporters his attempt on Mrs. Burbank had failed and asked for life imprisonment.
After a preliminary examination before Justice Bosard, Sheriff Jenks took Thurber to the county jail, and the crowd, which had reached 1,000, turned on it.
The Grand Forks Herald wrote that the vigilance committee did not lead this rush; the most active men were railroad men and friends of Conductor Burbank, who told them to 'take him out and hang him'.
The officers fought off battering rams, axes and ropes with their clubs, and a plan to burn the jail was dropped because four other prisoners were inside.
The keys were taken from Sheriff Jenks in the struggle, and at 3:45 the doors gave way before a crowd the Pioneer Press put at 3,000.
Thurber was dragged out with a noose, half strangled, and carried to the railroad bridge.
There, with crowds on the banks and bluffs below, Burbank was called for and placed the noose, and Thurber was thrown off at about 4 p.m.
The Herald reported that men on the bridge drank 'to his health' as he died; the body was cut down at 5:30.
The Associated Press reported that all the officers were injured, some severely, and that many in the mob were badly hurt by clubs.
The Pioneer Press said an inquest was 'probable', but no report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.
Later notes said Mrs. Burbank was recovering and that a Wisconsin prison warden had written that Thurber had served two terms for rape.
White papers repeated the accusation as fact and called Thurber a 'brute', 'fiend' and 'ravisher'.

The St. Paul Globe's own correspondent wrote that 'the feelings of the community fully justify the act', and the paper's editorial 'A Just Retribution' called rape the one crime for which lynch law was 'fully justifiable'.
The Globe and the Jamestown Alert both argued that a death penalty for rape would end lynching, and the Mankato Free Press called it 'A JUSTIFYABLE case of lynching'.
The Grand Forks Herald, reprinted under the Bismarck headline 'Hung With Hilarity and Dispatch', called the death 'sickening and disgusting' while using a slur for Thurber.

The first wire said the girl was a Norwegian 'ravished' on the road, while Buxton Blade editor Sam Treadwell said she was Minnie Tepka, a German girl whom Thurber threw down but 'failed to accomplish his design'.
Thurber told the Pioneer Press his attempt on Mrs. Burbank had also failed, while a later Herald item said there had been two struggles 'much more severe than at first represented'.
Crowd counts range from 200 to 3,000, and one brief placed the lynching at Norton.

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: Before the capture, the wire said a Black barber had 'ravished' a Norwegian girl on the road and 'outraged' Mrs. Burbank, and would 'undoubtedly be lynched if caught'.

accounts.label: Associated Press and Globe special
accounts.gist: After a hearing he was put in the county jail, which a mob of 2,000 stormed after a hard fight with officers, then hanged him from the railroad bridge.

accounts.label: Pioneer Press correspondent
accounts.gist: A night raid on the city jail was called off; next afternoon a crowd that grew to 3,000 broke into the county jail at 3:45 and hanged him at 4 p.m., Burbank placing the noose.

accounts.label: Grand Forks Herald
accounts.gist: The vigilance committee had planned an 'orderly' hanging after a hearing, but an unorganized crowd led by railroad men acted first; the hanging was watched from the bluffs amid jeers and drinking.

accounts.label: Thurber's own statements (as reported)
accounts.gist: In his cell he told reporters he did not know what made him do it, that his attempt on Mrs. Burbank had failed, and asked for life imprisonment instead of death.

accounts.label: Buxton Blade editor
accounts.gist: Treadwell said Thurber drove to the girl's father's farm, threw her down, and 'failed to accomplish his design' when her mother and field hands ran up.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Globe's correspondent wrote that 'the feelings of the community fully justify the act' and its editorial 'A Just Retribution' called rape 'the one crime' where lynch law was 'fully justifiable'.
The Mankato Free Press called it 'A JUSTIFYABLE case of lynching' and the Jamestown Alert said the proof of guilt was positive and urged a death penalty for rape.

The Grand Forks Herald, under the headline 'Hung With Hilarity and Dispatch', described the death agony as 'sickening and disgusting' while calling the victim a 'coon' and the crowd's spirit 'poetical justice'.
Distant papers ran one-line briefs in news-summary columns, calling him a negro who outraged 'two respectable white women'.

conflicts.note: All refer to one man; the early wire names are garbled and later reports settle on Thurber.
Counts were given at different moments of the afternoon.
Norton is where the alleged assault on Mrs. Burbank occurred; the Kenosha brief conflates it with the lynching site.
The on-the-spot dispatches give Oct. 24 at 4 p.m.
